To form the past infinitive: avoir / être + past participle.
To use “après avoir… / après être…” for an earlier action.
To put a story in order: d’abord, ensuite, puis, enfin, finalement.
To describe a traditional wedding and its customs.

Sunday, 15 August, the Feast of the Assumption. The grandmother’s house, in the village. It’s 7 a.m. and everyone is already up. Karim and Leïla, the godparents, have come from Lyon. The grandmother is giving orders, Ioana is translating.
Ioana, your grandmother has been talking for twenty minutes. What’s she saying?
She’s explaining the programme. First, before going to the church, everyone has to eat. She says you don’t get married on an empty stomach.
Then, after eating, the godparents have to come and fetch the bride and groom. That’s you, Karim and Leïla. You have to bring the candles and an embroidered towel.
Candles? We’ve got them! We bought them yesterday, after arriving in Iași. They’re enormous!
And me? What do I have to do before leaving?
(laughing) The young people of the village are going to hide the bride. It’s the tradition. After looking for her, you’ll have to pay to get her back. With money… or with țuică.
They’re going to steal my wife? Even before the ceremony?
No, after. After coming out of the church, during the party. Don’t worry, Radu promised me he wouldn’t hide me too far away.
Radu? Radu is organising this? Then I’m done for.
And during the ceremony, what happens? I’ve never been to an Orthodox wedding.
The priest blesses the rings, then he puts crowns on the heads of the bride and groom. Then they walk around the altar table three times, with the godparents. It’s very beautiful.
Three times? With an enormous candle in my hand? I’ll practise before we leave.
(she looks at Julien, who winks at her) And finally, after dancing the hora, after eating, after paying for the bride… we’ll have a little announcement to make. But that’s a surprise.
to have (“après avoir mangé” = after eating)
to be (“après être arrivés” = after arriving)
go (“vont cacher” = are going to hide)
to have her (“après l’avoir cherchée” = after looking for her)
goes (“on va voler” = they’re going to steal)
“A-preh-za-vwar”: liaison with z between après and avoir.
“A-vã duh par-teer”: the e in “de” almost disappears: “a-vãd-par-teer”.
“See-erzh”: the big church candle. An ordinary candle is “la bougie”.
“Pa-rẽ” / “ma-ren”: the masculine is nasal, the feminine isn’t.
“A-sõp-syõ”: 15 August, a public holiday in France too. The p is barely pronounced.
“Avant de” + infinitive = before doing something. The subject of the two actions is the SAME:
I wash my hands before eating.
Karim is going to practise before going to the church.
Different subjects → “avant que” + subjunctive (ch. 26): “Partons avant qu’il pleuve.” Same subject → “avant de” + infinitive: “Partons avant de manger.”
Past infinitive = AVOIR or ÊTRE (infinitive) + PAST PARTICIPLE. The auxiliary is chosen exactly as in the passé composé:
With “être”, the participle agrees with the subject: “Après être arrivéS, ils ont dansé.” “Après être sortiE, elle a souri.”
“Après” + PAST infinitive = after having done something. Careful: in careful French you DON’T say “après manger”, but “après avoir mangé”.
We bought them after arriving in Iași.
After dancing the hora, we’ll make an announcement.
She rested after doing her make-up.
English often says “after + -ing” (“after eating”). French needs the past infinitive: “après avoir mangé” — literally “after having eaten”.
“Enfin” = the last in a list OR “at last!” (after waiting). “Finalement” = in the end (the result was different from what you expected).

For a French person, a Romanian wedding is impressive: it lasts all night, there are hundreds of guests, and the godparents play a much bigger role than French “témoins”. They remain the couple’s “spiritual parents” for life.

The little village church was full long before the bride and groom arrived. There were cousins from all over Moldavia, neighbours, children in their Sunday best, and even the village mayor, who hadn’t missed a single wedding in forty years.

Ioana was wearing her grandmother’s embroidered blouse, with a long white skirt. Before going into the church, her grandmother looked at her for a long time. Then she said something in Romanian that Ioana didn’t want to translate. She had tears in her eyes.

The ceremony lasted an hour and a quarter. After blessing the rings, the priest placed the crowns on the heads of the bride and groom. Then they walked around the altar table three times, followed by Karim and Leïla, each holding a candle as tall as themselves.

On the second round, the wax from Karim’s candle dripped onto his shoe. He said nothing, but his face was so comical that Radu had to go outside the church to laugh. Brigitte, for her part, had been crying since the beginning, without understanding a single word.

After coming out of the church, the newlyweds were greeted by a shower of wheat grains and sweets. Then the whole village formed a big hora in front of the church. Pierre, who had learnt the steps at the wedding in Lyon, danced like a real Romanian.

The party took place in the grandmother’s yard, under a huge white tent. There were a hundred and fifty guests, three musicians with an accordion, a violin and a cimbalom, and enough food to feed an army.

At about ten in the evening, while Julien was talking to the mayor, the lights went out. When they came back on, Ioana had disappeared. The whole tent cheered. Radu climbed onto a chair. “The bride has been stolen! To get her back, the groom must pay!”

Julien searched everywhere: in the kitchen, in the garden, behind the barn. After searching for twenty minutes, he found Ioana in the cellar, sitting on a barrel, surrounded by five laughing cousins. They wanted three bottles of țuică and a song.
Dan had prepared the bottles that morning. Julien sang the song in Romanian, with a terrible accent: “Mulți ani trăiască”. The cousins applauded and gave him back his wife.

At midnight, after eating the cake, after dancing until they could no longer feel their feet, Ioana and Julien climbed onto the musicians’ little stage. Ioana took the microphone. The music stopped. A hundred and fifty faces turned towards them.

“Thank you all for coming,” she said, first in Romanian, then in French. “Before we carry on with the party, we have a little announcement to make.” She looked at Julien. Julien took the little scan photo out of his pocket and held it up high.
“In March,” said Ioana, her voice trembling, “there will be a new member of this family.”

For a second there was total silence. Then everything exploded at once. Elena screamed. Brigitte screamed louder. Dan knocked over his chair. Pierre hugged Dan as if they had known each other forever. Manon started to cry. Radu stood there with his mouth open, then he yelled: “I’m going to be an uncle!”
But the quickest was the grandmother. Before the others had even stood up, she was already on the stage. She took Ioana’s face in both hands and said, very softly, in Romanian: “Știam.” I knew.

“How?” asked Ioana. “Nobody told you!” The grandmother smiled. “This morning, when you put on the blouse, it was a little tight at the waist. And you didn’t drink any coffee. I was young once too, you know.”

The party started again, even louder. The musicians played until dawn. And at five in the morning, as the sun was rising over the hills, Julien asked the musicians if they knew a waltz. They didn’t. So he took the accordion and played Henri’s waltz himself, the way his grandfather Marcel had taught him.

Ioana danced with her father. Then with Pierre. Then with Radu. And finally with her grandmother, who declared, after dancing, that she had never seen a Frenchman play the accordion so well. It was probably true. He was also the first Frenchman she had ever seen play the accordion.

At about six in the morning, when the last guests had left, the family found themselves alone in the yard, around a table covered in leftovers. Nobody wanted to go to bed. The sun was slowly rising over the hills, and the village roosters were starting to crow.

Dan brought out one last bottle, very old and covered in dust. “I was keeping it for the birth of my first grandchild,” he explained. “I didn’t think I’d open it so soon.” He filled the glasses, and for Ioana, a glass of grape juice.

Brigitte and Elena were holding hands. They didn’t need a translator. They were already talking about names, with gestures, with three words of English, with lots of laughter. Brigitte suggested French names, Elena Romanian names, and the grandmother shook her head at every suggestion.

“And you, what do you suggest?” Ioana asked her grandmother. The old lady thought for a long time. Then she answered: “If it’s a girl, call her whatever you like. But before you choose, ask Hélène. She waited sixty years to have a family. She deserves to give her opinion.”

Ioana translated for Julien. Julien looked at the grandmother, then at Ioana, and smiled. He said nothing. But in the little music notebook, the one he had bought for the baby, he wrote a new line that morning, under the lullaby: “Maybe… Hélène?”

Reading text: A guide to the Romanian wedding
Leïla found a guide online for French guests at a Romanian wedding. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Invited to a wedding in Romania? Congratulations! Here are a few tips for surviving the longest party of your life.
First, before leaving, get a good night’s sleep. A Romanian wedding often starts in the morning and ends the next day at dawn.
Next, the religious ceremony. After going into the church, stay standing: there are often no chairs. It lasts about an hour.
After congratulating the bride and groom, you’ll go to the restaurant. Watch out: you’ll be served at least six courses, and each course will be followed by dancing.
During the evening, the bride may be “stolen” by friends. The groom will have to find her and pay a ransom. Don’t worry, it’s a game.
Finally, around midnight, after eating the cake, the guests give their present: usually an envelope with money, handed directly to the godparents.
Last but not least, the most important tip: before saying no to a glass of țuică, think carefully. Saying no is almost impossible.
